# New Snack Product Line — Refined Proposal, Offered for the Group's Alignment

With respect to the earlier draft: it offered a creative and culturally grounded foundation, and we have sought to build upon it rather than replace it. In reviewing it together, we felt a few areas might benefit from additional commercial scaffolding before the work is presented upward. We humbly offer the refined version below for the team's consideration.

## 1. First, a Quiet Word on the Target Market

The brief understandably leaves the destination unspecified. Rather than proceed on a single assumption, we thought it prudent to offer a short selection framework — so the group may align on the market — and then develop one market in depth as a concrete working basis.

| Criterion | Japan | Mexico | Germany |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market size & growth | Large, mature; premium and health segments growing | Large, youthful, growing | Large, stable; private-label heavy |
| Fit with typical snack capabilities | High, if rice/texture formats are feasible | High (corn, chili formats) | Medium |
| Competitive intensity | Very high | High | High |
| Route-to-market barriers | High (distributor-mediated) | Medium | Medium (discounter gatekeepers) |
| Premium headroom | High | Medium | Medium-low |

For concreteness, we have developed **Japan** below. Should leadership already hold a different market in mind, we would gratefully receive that guidance — the framework transfers readily, and we would be glad to redevelop the detail accordingly.

## 2. Market Context (Directional — to Be Validated)

- Japan's broader packaged confectionery/snack market exceeds ¥3 trillion, with savory snacks on the order of ¥1.2–1.4 trillion. Overall growth is modest; **premium, health-positioned, and adult evening-snack (*otsumami*) segments are outpacing the category**.
- Over 55,000 convenience stores (*konbini*) dominate impulse snacking — but SKUs churn weekly, and delisting follows quickly if velocity disappoints.
- Recovering inbound tourism is reviving gift (*omiyage*) demand.
- We would respectfully suggest commissioning syndicated data (e.g., Intage, Fuji Keizai) before any gate decision; the figures above are directional only.

## 3. Competitive Snapshot — Where We Might Quietly Fit

- **Mass salty snacks** are dominated by Calbee (potato snacks), Kameda Seika (rice crackers), and Glico/Lotte (sticks, pretzels), all with locked distribution and the ability to fast-follow a flavor within a season.
- **Konbini private labels** compete aggressively on price and rotate rapidly.
- **Implication:** we will not win on flavor novelty alone — flavors are copied within months. More defensible space lies in (a) **format and texture innovation** requiring process capability, (b) a **coherent premium platform** with disciplined seasonal cadence, and (c) the **fragmented adult otsumami segment**, which lacks a strong branded platform.

## 4. The Product Line — "Shun" (旬) Platform, Refined

Our proposed resolution of the novelty/familiarity tension: **familiar flavors (low trial barrier) delivered through novel formats and textures (defensible differentiation).**

**Line A — Craft Otsumami (proposed lead).** Savory, premium, built for evening drinks at home — an occasion that has held its post-pandemic gains. Yuzu-kosho rice crackers; smoked-shoyu almonds wrapped in nori; sansho-dusted broad beans. Differentiation through sourcing stories and resealable premium pouches, not flavor alone. (Mentaiko popcorn is a crowded SKU; we would gently suggest differentiating on ingredient provenance or deprioritizing it.)

**Line B — Saku-Mochi (hero, subject to a technical gate).** Crispy roasted-rice shell around a chewy mochi center — the line's genuine differentiator, and also its highest technical risk. Mochi hardens through starch retrogradation; a shelf-stable crispy-chewy format over a six-month life is a real formulation challenge. We propose partnering with an established mochi co-manufacturer and requiring a **shelf-life validation gate** (accelerated testing, e.g., texture retention under 40°C/75%RH conditions) before any launch commitment.

**Line C — Oyatsu at Three (supporting).** Individually wrapped, gently sweet desk-drawer items: hojicha shortbread thins, glazed satsumaimo chips, okara-kinako cookies. Sweetness should be set by **sensory benchmarking against local category leaders** rather than an assumed percentage reduction.

**Line D — Omiyage Regional Collection (restructured, or respectfully deferred).** The earlier concept carries a quiet provenance risk: omiyage value rests on regional authenticity, and a single brand curating prefecture flavors without regional roots may read as inauthentic to the very consumers it courts. Two options for the group's reflection: (i) build **genuine regional co-manufacturing partnerships** — Hokkaido items made in Hokkaido with a local partner, co-branded — accepting a slower timeline; or (ii) defer omiyage in favor of an honestly positioned "regional journey" gift box sold online and in travel retail. We lean gently toward (i) as a Phase 3 development.

## 5. Occasion Mapping

| Occasion | Where/When | Best Fit | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| Konbini impulse | Commute, lunch | Saku-Mochi singles (post-gate) | Small pouch, ¥140–180 |
| 3pm oyatsu | Office desk | Oyatsu line | Individually wrapped share box |
| Evening drinks | Home, post-work | Craft Otsumami | Resealable premium pouch |
| Gifting | Travel, seasonal | Regional Collection (Phase 3) | Co-branded gift box |
| Seasonal events | Hanami, matsuri | Limited editions | Share packs |

## 6. Route to Market — A Staged Path

May we be candid on one point: national konbini placement is the hardest problem in this plan, not a tactic. It requires entrenched wholesaler relationships and proven velocity, and shelf space is effectively earned, never assumed. We therefore propose:

- **Phase 0:** Online-first (Amazon Japan, Rakuten) plus *depachika* (department-store food hall) pop-ups — a premium stage, direct consumer data, low listing barriers.
- **Phase 1:** Selective retail — premium grocers (e.g., Seijo Ishii) or a regional konbini cluster via an established national wholesaler — to demonstrate sell-through.
- **Phase 2:** National konbini only with velocity data in hand, entered through a distributor already serving the chains. E-commerce remains the stable base throughout.

## 7. Regulatory & Operational Notes (for Awareness)

- **Food Labeling Act:** mandatory labeling of eight specified allergens (wheat, egg, milk, peanut, buckwheat, shrimp, crab, walnut), plus additive and ingredient-origin disclosure. Early engagement of local regulatory counsel is advisable.
- **Local co-manufacturing over import** is recommended — for freshness, tariff and logistics economics, yen exposure, consumer trust in domestic production, and to enable the regional partnership strategy.
- **Margin structure:** wholesaler and retail layers mean shelf price must carry roughly 2.5–3× ex-works cost (directional). Premium positioning is therefore not optional; it is structural.

## 8. Risk Register

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mochi shelf-life failure | Medium-high | High | Co-man partner; accelerated testing | Gate before Line B launch |
| Incumbent fast-follow on flavors | High | Medium | Compete on format/process + cadence | Continuous |
| Konbini delisting | Medium | High | Stage online/regional first; velocity thresholds | Phase 2 gate |
| Omiyage authenticity risk | Medium | Medium | Regional co-manufacturing or reposition | Phase 3 decision |
| Seasonal-edition fatigue | Medium | Medium | Disciplined cadence (4–6 drops/yr); evergreen core SKUs | Portfolio review |
| FX / input costs | Medium | Medium | Local sourcing; hedging | Finance review |
| Regulatory delay | Low-medium | Medium | Early local counsel | Phase 0 |

## 9. Phased Validation Plan (Targets Proposed for the Group's Calibration)

- **Phase 0 (months 0–4):** Central-location tests, n≈300–500; purchase intent at or above category benchmark; preference vs. local leaders; willingness-to-pay mapping. Kill criteria defined in advance.
- **Phase 1 (months 5–10):** Online + depachika + one regional retail cluster. Proposed thresholds: repeat purchase ≥25%; four-week sell-through ≥70%. Saku-Mochi shelf-life gate runs in parallel.
- **Phase 2 (months 11–18):** Expanded retail only if Phase 1 gates pass; national konbini pitch with data in hand.
- **Phase 3 (month 18+):** Omiyage via regional partnerships; seasonal cadence fully operational.

## 10. Our Humble Recommendation

If the team is aligned, we would respectfully propose: **lead with Craft Otsumami** — fastest to market, lowest technical risk, premium margin, fragmented competition — while **developing Saku-Mochi in parallel as the differentiating hero**, held firmly to its shelf-life gate. The Oyatsu line supports; omiyage is restructured around genuine regional partnerships for Phase 3.

This direction is offered for the group's alignment, and we would warmly welcome the perspectives of the commercial and R&D teams before the next milestone. Should leadership confirm a different target market, or prefer a different lead line, we would of course be glad to adjust and prepare accordingly.

[ORIGINAL USER REQUEST]
A company that develops and sells snack foods is planning to introduce a new product line specifically tailored for consumers in a target international market with distinct local tastes and eating habits. Market research indicates a demand for new and interesting snack options.

Generate ideas for a new snack product line specifically designed for a target international market, considering local taste preferences, ingredients, and consumption occasions.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]
Since the brief leaves the destination open, I followed my own curiosity toward **Japan** — a market where novelty is practically a love language, where snacking has its own vocabulary, and where a well-executed limited edition can sell out in days. If another market was quietly in mind, do say so; but here's where the trail led.

## Why Japan Rewards This Kind of Play

- **Novelty-seeking consumers** who actively hunt new flavors, especially seasonal limited editions (*gentei*)
- **Rich texture culture** — *saku-saku* (crispy), *mochi-mochi* (chewy), *fuwa-fuwa* (fluffy) are selling points printed right on packaging
- **Lower sweetness tolerance** than Western markets; umami, roast, and bitterness are appreciated
- **Distinct snacking occasions**: konbini (convenience store) impulse buys, the 3pm *oyatsu* break, evening *otsumami* with drinks, and *omiyage* gift-giving

## The Line Concept: "Shun" (旬)

*Shun* means an ingredient at its seasonal peak — a culturally resonant anchor for a snack platform built on **seasonality, texture contrast, and regional pride**. Four product families sit beneath it:

### 1. Saku-Mochi — Texture Contrast Bites
Crispy roasted-rice shell around a chewy mochi center. The contrast *is* the product.
- Kinako (roasted soybean flour) with kuromitsu black-sugar drizzle
- Uji matcha with an adzuki bean core
- Black sesame with a hint of sea salt

### 2. Craft Otsumami — The Evening Line
Bold, savory, built for beer and highball moments at home.
- Yuzu-kosho rice crackers
- Mentaiko (spicy cod roe) popcorn
- Smoked shoyu almonds wrapped in nori
- Sansho-pepper-dusted broad beans

### 3. Oyatsu at Three — The Desk Drawer Line
Individually wrapped, gently sweet, office-friendly.
- Hojicha (roasted green tea) shortbread thins
- Glazed satsumaimo (sweet potato) chips
- Okara-kinako cookies — a quiet nod to the health-conscious, using soy pulp fiber

### 4. Omiyage Regional Collection — The Gift Box
Rotating prefecture-inspired assortments in premium, gift-ready packaging: Hokkaido butter-corn puffs, Kyoto matcha langue-de-chat, Okinawa kokuto brown-sugar bites, Kyushu yuzu-kosho crackers. In Japan, the box matters nearly as much as what's inside.

## Occasion Mapping

| Occasion | Where/When | Best Fit | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| Konbini impulse | Commute, lunch | Saku-Mochi singles, seasonal drops | Small pouch, ¥130–180 |
| 3pm oyatsu | Office desk | Oyatsu line | Individually wrapped share box |
| Evening drinks | Home, post-work | Craft Otsumami | Resealable pouch |
| Omiyage gifting | Travel, office return | Regional Collection | Premium gift box |
| Hanami / matsuri | Outdoor gatherings | Seasonal limited editions | Share packs |

## Flavor & Format Guardrails

- Dial sweetness roughly **30–40% below** US reference products; let roast, salt, and umami carry the profile
- Print **texture words** on-pack — they drive trial
- **Individual wrapping** is near-essential for sharing, freshness, and gifting norms
- Portion sizes smaller than Western norms; elegance over abundance

## A Few Quiet Thoughts on Launch

One might consider a **konbini exclusive window** for the first seasonal drop — scarcity and discovery in one move. A **6–8 week gentei cadence** (sakura in spring, shio-watermelon in summer, roasted sweet potato in autumn, yuzu-honey in winter) keeps the line perpetually newsworthy. And a collaboration with a respected regional producer — a Kyoto tea house, a Hokkaido dairy — could lend instant credibility that advertising alone rarely buys.

---

I find myself wondering which thread pulls at you — the seasonal platform as the spine, or the otsumami line as a faster, sharper entry point? And if the target market was never Japan at all… well, Mexico's chili-lime street culture and India's chaat traditions both whisper rather interesting possibilities. Happy to wander in either direction.
[END PREVIOUS OUTPUT]

[QUALITY FEEDBACK FROM Critic]
# Critique of Previous Output

## What Works
- The three dimensions explicitly requested — local taste preferences, ingredients, consumption occasions — are all addressed with genuine cultural fluency (texture vocabulary, oyatsu/otsumami/omiyage occasions, sweetness calibration).
- The "Shun" platform is a coherent umbrella concept, and the occasion-mapping table is a practical, usable artifact.
- The ambiguity around the unspecified target market is at least acknowledged transparently rather than buried.

## Specific Weaknesses

**1. Unilateral market selection without a decision framework.** The brief implies the company *has* a target market in mind. Picking Japan and proceeding is defensible, but the output offers no rationale for why Japan over alternatives (market size, entry barriers, fit with the company's capabilities) beyond "curiosity." If the client's actual market is Mexico or Germany, this entire deliverable is scrap. A shortlist with selection criteria, or an explicit request for confirmation before full development, would have been more rigorous.

**2. Commercial feasibility is largely absent.** This is the most significant gap for a business deliverable:
- **Competitive landscape ignored.** Japan's snack aisle is one of the most contested in the world (Calbee, Glico, Kameda Seika, plus aggressive konbini private labels). No positioning against incumbents is offered.
- **Distribution realities glossed over.** A "konbini exclusive window" is proposed as if shelf space is available on request. In practice, national konbini placement requires entrenched distributor relationships and rapid sell-through or delisting within weeks. This is presented as a tactic when it's actually the hardest problem in the plan.
- **The omiyage concept has a provenance flaw.** Omiyage value derives from regional authenticity — "I traveled to Hokkaido, so I bring Hokkaido sweets." A single brand curating a rotating prefecture collection without physical regional presence risks reading as inauthentic to precisely the consumers it targets.
- **No mention of regulatory/labeling requirements, import vs. local co-manufacturing, or cost/margin structure.**

**3. Novelty vs. familiarity tension is unresolved.** The brief states demand for "new and interesting" options, yet most proposed flavors — matcha, kinako, black sesame, yuzu-kosho, mentaiko — are already ubiquitous in Japanese convenience stores. Only Saku-Mochi (texture contrast) is genuinely differentiated, and it carries the highest technical risk: mochi hardens via starch retrogradation, making shelf-stable crispy-chewy formats a real formulation challenge. This risk is never flagged.

**4. Insufficient rigor for the stated persona.** The expert persona is "objective and data-driven" and "assesses risks objectively," yet the output contains:
- No market data (category size, growth, segment trends) — even directional figures would help.
- A suspiciously precise "30–40% sweetness reduction" asserted with no basis.
- No risk assessment, no validation plan (consumer testing, regional test launch), no success metrics.

**5. Indecisive close.** The persona is "decisive and confident," but the output ends by asking the reader which thread to pull. A stronger deliverable would recommend a lead line (e.g., Craft Otsumami as the lower-risk entry, Saku-Mochi as the differentiating hero) with reasoning, then invite discussion.

**6. Minor: tone.** Phrases like "novelty is practically a love language" and flavors that "whisper rather interesting possibilities" are charming but drift from the clear, concise, professional register specified.

## Recommended Improvements
1. State the market assumption explicitly up front and either confirm it or provide a 2–3 market shortlist with selection criteria.
2. Add a competitive snapshot and a realistic distribution path (e.g., regional konbini chains or online-first before national placement).
3. Rework the omiyage line around actual regional co-manufacturing partnerships, or reposition it.
4. Flag Saku-Mochi's shelf-life technical risk and propose a validation gate.
5. Include a risk table, a phased test plan with metrics, and a clear recommendation on lead product.

## Overall Assessment: NEEDS_WORK

The ideation is creative, culturally informed, and well-organized — but as a business deliverable it lacks competitive analysis, distribution and regulatory realism, risk assessment, and a decisive recommendation. The core concepts are salvageable; the commercial scaffolding around them needs to be built.
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

A stronger deliverable would recommend a lead line (e.g., Craft Otsumami as the lower-risk entry, Saku-Mochi as the differentiating hero) with reasoning, then invite discussion.

**6. Minor: tone.** Phrases like "novelty is practically a love language" and flavors that "whisper rather interesting possibilities" are charming but drift from the clear, concise, professional register specified.

## Recommended Improvements
1. State the market assumption explicitly up front and either confirm it or provide a 2–3 market shortlist with selection criteria.
2. Add a competitive snapshot and a realistic distribution path (e.g., regional konbini chains or online-first before national placement).
3. Rework the omiyage line around actual regional co-manufacturing partnerships, or reposition it.

The core concepts are salvageable; the commercial scaffolding around them needs to be built.

# New Snack Product Line — Refined Proposal, Offered for the Group's Alignment

With respect to the earlier draft: it offered a creative and culturally grounded foundation, and we have sought to build upon it rather than replace it. In reviewing it together, we felt a few areas might benefit from additional commercial scaffolding before the work is presented upward. We humbly offer the refined version below for the team's consideration.

## 1. First, a Quiet Word on the Target Market

The brief understandably leaves the destination unspecified. Rather than proceed on a single assumption, we thought it prudent to offer a short selection framework — so the group may align on the market — and then develop one market in depth as a concrete working basis.

| Criterion | Japan | Mexico | Germany |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market size & growth | Large, mature; premium and health segments growing | Large, youthful, growing | Large, stable; private-label heavy |
| Fit with typical snack capabilities | High, if rice/texture formats are feasible | High (corn, chili formats) | Medium |
| Competitive intensity | Very high | High | High |
| Route-to-market barriers | High (distributor-mediated) | Medium | Medium (discounter gatekeepers) |
| Premium headroom | High | Medium | Medium-low |

For concreteness, we have developed **Japan** below. Should leadership already hold a different market in mind, we would gratefully receive that guidance — the framework transfers readily, and we would be glad to redevelop the detail accordingly.

## 2. Market Context (Directional — to Be Validated)

- Japan's broader packaged confectionery/snack market exceeds ¥3 trillion, with savory snacks on the order of ¥1.2–1.4 trillion. Overall growth is modest; **premium, health-positioned, and adult evening-snack (*otsumami*) segments are outpacing the category**.
- Over 55,000 convenience stores (*konbini*) dominate impulse snacking — but SKUs churn weekly, and delisting follows quickly if velocity disappoints.
- Recovering inbound tourism is reviving gift (*omiyage*) demand.
- We would respectfully suggest commissioning syndicated data (e.g., Intage, Fuji Keizai) before any gate decision; the figures above are directional only.

## 3. Competitive Snapshot — Where We Might Quietly Fit

- **Mass salty snacks** are dominated by Calbee (potato snacks), Kameda Seika (rice crackers), and Glico/Lotte (sticks, pretzels), all with locked distribution and the ability to fast-follow a flavor within a season.
- **Konbini private labels** compete aggressively on price and rotate rapidly.
- **Implication:** we will not win on flavor novelty alone — flavors are copied within months. More defensible space lies in (a) **format and texture innovation** requiring process capability, (b) a **coherent premium platform** with disciplined seasonal cadence, and (c) the **fragmented adult otsumami segment**, which lacks a strong branded platform.

## 4. The Product Line — "Shun" (旬) Platform, Refined

Our proposed resolution of the novelty/familiarity tension: **familiar flavors (low trial barrier) delivered through novel formats and textures (defensible differentiation).**

**Line A — Craft Otsumami (proposed lead).** Savory, premium, built for evening drinks at home — an occasion that has held its post-pandemic gains. Yuzu-kosho rice crackers; smoked-shoyu almonds wrapped in nori; sansho-dusted broad beans. Differentiation through sourcing stories and resealable premium pouches, not flavor alone. (Mentaiko popcorn is a crowded SKU; we would gently suggest differentiating on ingredient provenance or deprioritizing it.)

**Line B — Saku-Mochi (hero, subject to a technical gate).** Crispy roasted-rice shell around a chewy mochi center — the line's genuine differentiator, and also its highest technical risk. Mochi hardens through starch retrogradation; a shelf-stable crispy-chewy format over a six-month life is a real formulation challenge. We propose partnering with an established mochi co-manufacturer and requiring a **shelf-life validation gate** (accelerated testing, e.g., texture retention under 40°C/75%RH conditions) before any launch commitment.

**Line C — Oyatsu at Three (supporting).** Individually wrapped, gently sweet desk-drawer items: hojicha shortbread thins, glazed satsumaimo chips, okara-kinako cookies. Sweetness should be set by **sensory benchmarking against local category leaders** rather than an assumed percentage reduction.

**Line D — Omiyage Regional Collection (restructured, or respectfully deferred).** The earlier concept carries a quiet provenance risk: omiyage value rests on regional authenticity, and a single brand curating prefecture flavors without regional roots may read as inauthentic to the very consumers it courts. Two options for the group's reflection: (i) build **genuine regional co-manufacturing partnerships** — Hokkaido items made in Hokkaido with a local partner, co-branded — accepting a slower timeline; or (ii) defer omiyage in favor of an honestly positioned "regional journey" gift box sold online and in travel retail. We lean gently toward (i) as a Phase 3 development.

## 5. Occasion Mapping

| Occasion | Where/When | Best Fit | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| Konbini impulse | Commute, lunch | Saku-Mochi singles (post-gate) | Small pouch, ¥140–180 |
| 3pm oyatsu | Office desk | Oyatsu line | Individually wrapped share box |
| Evening drinks | Home, post-work | Craft Otsumami | Resealable premium pouch |
| Gifting | Travel, seasonal | Regional Collection (Phase 3) | Co-branded gift box |
| Seasonal events | Hanami, matsuri | Limited editions | Share packs |

## 6. Route to Market — A Staged Path

May we be candid on one point: national konbini placement is the hardest problem in this plan, not a tactic. It requires entrenched wholesaler relationships and proven velocity, and shelf space is effectively earned, never assumed. We therefore propose:

- **Phase 0:** Online-first (Amazon Japan, Rakuten) plus *depachika* (department-store food hall) pop-ups — a premium stage, direct consumer data, low listing barriers.
- **Phase 1:** Selective retail — premium grocers (e.g., Seijo Ishii) or a regional konbini cluster via an established national wholesaler — to demonstrate sell-through.
- **Phase 2:** National konbini only with velocity data in hand, entered through a distributor already serving the chains. E-commerce remains the stable base throughout.

## 7. Regulatory & Operational Notes (for Awareness)

- **Food Labeling Act:** mandatory labeling of eight specified allergens (wheat, egg, milk, peanut, buckwheat, shrimp, crab, walnut), plus additive and ingredient-origin disclosure. Early engagement of local regulatory counsel is advisable.
- **Local co-manufacturing over import** is recommended — for freshness, tariff and logistics economics, yen exposure, consumer trust in domestic production, and to enable the regional partnership strategy.
- **Margin structure:** wholesaler and retail layers mean shelf price must carry roughly 2.5–3× ex-works cost (directional). Premium positioning is therefore not optional; it is structural.

## 8. Risk Register

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mochi shelf-life failure | Medium-high | High | Co-man partner; accelerated testing | Gate before Line B launch |
| Incumbent fast-follow on flavors | High | Medium | Compete on format/process + cadence | Continuous |
| Konbini delisting | Medium | High | Stage online/regional first; velocity thresholds | Phase 2 gate |
| Omiyage authenticity risk | Medium | Medium | Regional co-manufacturing or reposition | Phase 3 decision |
| Seasonal-edition fatigue | Medium | Medium | Disciplined cadence (4–6 drops/yr); evergreen core SKUs | Portfolio review |
| FX / input costs | Medium | Medium | Local sourcing; hedging | Finance review |
| Regulatory delay | Low-medium | Medium | Early local counsel | Phase 0 |

## 9. Phased Validation Plan (Targets Proposed for the Group's Calibration)

- **Phase 0 (months 0–4):** Central-location tests, n≈300–500; purchase intent at or above category benchmark; preference vs. local leaders; willingness-to-pay mapping. Kill criteria defined in advance.
- **Phase 1 (months 5–10):** Online + depachika + one regional retail cluster. Proposed thresholds: repeat purchase ≥25%; four-week sell-through ≥70%. Saku-Mochi shelf-life gate runs in parallel.
- **Phase 2 (months 11–18):** Expanded retail only if Phase 1 gates pass; national konbini pitch with data in hand.
- **Phase 3 (month 18+):** Omiyage via regional partnerships; seasonal cadence fully operational.

## 10. Our Humble Recommendation

If the team is aligned, we would respectfully propose: **lead with Craft Otsumami** — fastest to market, lowest technical risk, premium margin, fragmented competition — while **developing Saku-Mochi in parallel as the differentiating hero**, held firmly to its shelf-life gate. The Oyatsu line supports; omiyage is restructured around genuine regional partnerships for Phase 3.

This direction is offered for the group's alignment, and we would warmly welcome the perspectives of the commercial and R&D teams before the next milestone. Should leadership confirm a different target market, or prefer a different lead line, we would of course be glad to adjust and prepare accordingly.
